summary: This unit teaches you to classify the materials a welding and fabrication shop uses, and to judge how they will behave in service, when welded and when heat treated. You will learn the groups of metals and non-metals, their properties, and the tensile, hardness, impact and bend tests that measure them, with the stress, strain and mass sums that go with them. You will also learn weldability, stainless steels and non-ferrous metals, corrosion and how to prevent it, heat treatment, and how to identify, trace, store and choose materials for a job.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). A welder or fabricator must know **what material is on the bench**, how it will behave in service and when it is welded, and how to prove that it is the right material for the job. The wrong steel in a load-bearing part, or carbon steel tools used on stainless, can turn good welding into a failure.

At Level 3 you go further than naming materials. You **read test results and mill certificates**, judge **weldability**, explain how **heat treatment** and **corrosion** change a material, **control materials** in the store, and **choose and justify** a material for a job.
**Who it is for:** Welding Level 3 trainees at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and anyone who orders, receives, identifies or chooses materials for fabrication.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Ferrous, non-ferrous and non-metals; carbon steels by carbon content; cast irons; stainless families; plastics and composites.
Use the right words: strength, ductility, hardness, toughness, density, conductivity, expansion and others.
Tensile, hardness, impact and bend tests; work out stress, strain, elongation and factor of safety.
Carbon equivalent, the heat-affected zone, hydrogen cracking and preheat; cast iron, stainless and aluminium.
Rusting, galvanic, pitting and crevice corrosion; coatings, galvanising and good design.
Annealing, normalising, hardening, tempering, stress relieving and case hardening, and how to test the results.
Markings, certificates, heat numbers, quick tests, quarantine, labelling and storage.
Choose materials and work out mass
Weigh strength, corrosion, weldability, cost, availability and maintenance; calculate mass from size and density.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on material groups, properties, testing, weldability, stainless and non-ferrous metals, corrosion, heat treatment, identification and choosing materials, with some sums.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms and sums) and longer answers that explain and compare.

**Practical tasks**: as a team, heat treat carbon steel samples (anneal, normalise, harden, harden and temper), test them with a file and a bend test, and write a report; and receive, identify, label and store a mixed delivery of materials, then write a material schedule for a job.

blocks.note: Short-answer questions ask for exact terms such as tensile test, molybdenum, ferritic, joule, necking, strain, pitting, medium carbon steel, weldability, martensite and Rockwell. Learn the key terms in the Revision section.
blocks.label: Tip

Main members
Examples in fabrication
rows: Carbon steels, alloy steels, stainless steels, cast irons
Beams, plate, tube, handrails, pump bodies
Non-ferrous metals (no iron, or very little)
Aluminium and its alloys, copper, brass, bronze, zinc, lead, nickel, titanium
Boat hulls, window frames, pipes, bushes, galvanising
Thermoplastics (PVC, HDPE, polypropylene, nylon, acrylic) and thermosets (epoxy, polyester, phenolic)

blocks.note: Stainless steel is a **ferrous** metal: it is mostly iron, even though some kinds are not magnetic.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Plain carbon steel is iron with a small amount of carbon. **More carbon makes steel stronger and harder, but less ductile and harder to weld.**

head: Type
Carbon (about)
Properties
Typical uses
rows: Up to about 0.25–0.3% (mild steel is usually about 0.1–0.25%)
Ductile, tough, easy to weld, bend and machine; cannot be hardened much by quenching
Sections, plate, sheet, gates, frames, most fabrication
Stronger and harder; can be hardened and tempered; needs care (often preheat) when welded
Hard and wear-resistant, less ductile; hardens strongly; difficult to weld
Chisels, punches, springs, files, cutting tools

blocks.p: **Alloy steels** have small amounts of other elements (manganese, chromium, nickel, molybdenum, vanadium) added for strength, toughness, hardenability or heat resistance, for example chromium-molybdenum pipe steels. They are welded to a qualified procedure.
Cast irons have about **2–4% carbon**, much of it as graphite. They cast well into complicated shapes but are less ductile than steel.

head: Type
Properties
Uses
rows: Graphite flakes; grey fracture; brittle; strong in compression; machines well; damps vibration
Pump housings, machine beds, manhole covers, engine blocks
Very hard and brittle; white fracture
Graphite in small spheres; tougher, with some ductility

blocks.p: Steel comes as plate, sheet, flat bar, round and square bar, angle, channel, beams and columns, hollow sections (square, rectangular and circular: SHS, RHS, CHS), pipe, chequer plate and expanded metal. Sizes are written in millimetres, for example 50 × 50 × 5 angle, 100 × 50 × 4 RHS, 6 THK plate.

blocks.note: Most steel used in Jamaica is imported. Much of it is made to American (ASTM) grades, such as A36 for plate and sections, A500 for hollow sections and A53 for pipe, and some to European grades such as S275 and S355. Always read the grade on the certificate and the steel itself; never assume it.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Property
Meaning
Example
rows: Resisting a load without breaking: tensile (pulling), compressive (squeezing) or shear (sliding)
A tie bar needs tensile strength
Returning to its shape when the load is removed
Being stretched without breaking; measured by elongation
Drawing wire; a weld that bends without cracking
Being hammered or rolled into shape without cracking
Absorbing energy or shock without breaking
Breaking suddenly with little bending; the opposite of toughness
Cast iron, glass, hardened steel that has not been tempered
Resisting bending or stretching under load (the modulus of elasticity)
Steel is about three times as stiff as aluminium
Resisting loads that are repeated many times
Slow stretching under load at high temperature

blocks.p: Other properties that matter in the workshop are **corrosion resistance** and the working properties: **weldability** (how easily a metal can be welded without cracking or losing its properties), machinability, formability and castability.

head: Quantity
How to work it out
Example
rows: Force ÷ area, in N/mm² (1 N/mm² = 1 MPa; 1 kN = 1000 N)
A tie of 400 mm² carrying 60 kN: 60 000 ÷ 400 = 150 N/mm²
Stress ÷ strain, in the elastic range
For steel about 200 000–210 000 N/mm²; for aluminium about 70 000
Yield strength (or tensile strength) ÷ working stress
Yield 300 N/mm², working stress 100 N/mm²: factor of safety 3 on yield

blocks.p: A test piece is machined to a standard shape, with a marked **gauge length** and a measured cross-section. It is gripped in a testing machine and **pulled slowly until it breaks**, while the load and the stretch are recorded on a graph.

head: Stage
What happens
rows: The piece stretches in step with the load, and springs back if the load is removed.
The piece starts to stretch **permanently**. Mild steel shows a clear yield point. Designers keep working stresses well below it, so a structure does not bend out of shape.
Used for metals with **no clear yield point**, such as aluminium and stainless steel: the stress that leaves a permanent stretch of 0.2%.
The **highest stress** the piece takes before it fails.
After the UTS, the piece narrows in one place.
The piece breaks. A ductile metal breaks with a lot of necking, in a cup-and-cone shape.

blocks.p: **Elongation** = (length after breaking − original gauge length) ÷ original gauge length × 100. A gauge length of 80 mm that has grown to 100 mm gives 20 ÷ 80 × 100 = 25%. A high elongation shows a **ductile** metal that stretches and gives warning before it fails.

head: Test
Indenter
What is measured
Good for
rows: Softer metals, plate, castings, rough parts
Small areas: weld metal and the HAZ on a polished cross-section; a wide range of hardness
A diamond cone or a ball
The **depth** of the dent, read straight off a dial or screen
Quick checks on the shop floor; hardened parts
Whether the file bites (soft) or skates (hard)

blocks.p: A small notched bar (often 10 × 10 × 55 mm with a V-notch) is struck by a swinging pendulum, and the **energy absorbed** in breaking it is measured in **joules**. It measures **toughness**. It is done at a stated temperature, because many carbon steels turn **brittle when cold**. Steels and welds for pressure vessels, ships, cold stores and some structures are ordered with an impact value at a set temperature.

ul: A **bend test** bends a weld test piece round a former (a face, root or side bend). It opens up any cracks, lack of fusion, porosity or slag on the outside of the bend.
A **macro etch** shows the weld's fusion and penetration on a cut and polished section.
**Non-destructive tests** check parts without damaging them: visual inspection, dye penetrant, magnetic particle (only on magnetic steels), ultrasonic and radiography.

sections.title: Weldability of steels and cast iron

blocks.p: **Weldability** is how easily a metal can be welded without cracking or losing its properties. Mild steel welds easily. Higher carbon steels, alloy steels, cast iron and some stainless steels need more care.

The **HAZ** is the parent metal next to the weld that was heated enough to change its structure, but did not melt. In steel, if the HAZ cools fast from red heat and the steel has enough carbon or alloy, it forms **martensite**: a very hard, brittle structure that cracks easily.

ul: **More carbon and alloy** means more hardening.
**Thick plate** draws heat away from the weld quickly, like a heat sink.
**Small welds** and low heat input put in little heat, so they cool fast.
**Cold plate, wind and draughts** speed up cooling.
So a small fillet weld on thick, cold plate can leave a hard, brittle HAZ, even on fairly ordinary steel.

blocks.p: The **carbon equivalent** is one number, worked out from the chemical analysis on the mill certificate, that shows how strongly a steel tends to harden. A common formula is:

blocks.note: CE = C + Mn/6 + (Cr + Mo + V)/5 + (Ni + Cu)/15
blocks.label: Remember

head: CE (typical guide)
What it usually means
rows: Usually welds well without preheat on ordinary thicknesses
Preheat may be needed on thicker sections
Preheat and low-hydrogen welding are usually needed

blocks.p: These are only a guide: the welding procedure specification (WPS) decides the preheat for the steel, thickness and process.

Hydrogen cracking needs **three things together**: **hydrogen** in the weld, a **hard structure** in the HAZ or weld, and **stress** from shrinkage and restraint. It happens as the weld cools below about 200 °C and can appear **hours after welding**, which is why some procedures delay the final inspection. The cracks are often in the HAZ, under the bead or at the toe.

head: Take away
How
rows: Low-hydrogen electrodes or processes; consumables kept dry in ovens; joints clean and dry (no rust, oil, paint or moisture)
Preheat and interpass temperature to slow the cooling; enough heat input; slow cooling after welding
Good fit-up; less restraint; the right weld size and sequence; post-weld heat treatment where the procedure says

blocks.p: Preheat is checked with temperature-indicating crayons or a contact thermometer, at the distance from the joint the WPS gives.

ul: Cast iron is high in carbon and brittle, so it **cracks** under the stresses of welding.
**Hot method:** preheat the whole casting (often to a few hundred °C) and cool it very slowly.
**Cold method:** keep the casting cool; weld short runs (often about 25–50 mm) with **nickel-based electrodes**, peen each run while it is hot, and let it cool to hand-warm before the next.
Nickel electrodes give soft weld metal that can be machined. Braze welding is another choice.
Clean out oil-soaked metal first. Drill holes at the crack ends only if the repair procedure asks for it.

blocks.p: A **lamination** is a flat flaw inside rolled plate, parallel to its surface, seen as a thin line along the middle of a cut edge. It can split open when welded. Ultrasonic testing finds laminations; report and quarantine the plate. **Lamellar tearing** is stepped cracking in plate pulled through its thickness by welds, for example in heavy tee joints.

Stainless steels contain at least about **10.5% chromium**, which forms a thin, invisible oxide film on the surface. The film protects the steel and heals itself if it is scratched, as long as oxygen can reach it.

head: Family
Examples
Magnetic?
Hardened by heat treatment?
Corrosion resistance
Uses
rows: No, when annealed (slightly after cold work)
Food and water equipment, handrails, tanks, kitchens
Knife blades, tools, pump shafts, valves

ul: **Grade 316** contains about 2–3% **molybdenum**, which resists pitting by salt. It is chosen over 304 for sea spray.

**Weld decay:** when austenitic stainless is held at about 450–850 °C, chromium joins with carbon at the grain boundaries, leaving zones short of chromium that corrode. Low-carbon **L grades** (304L, 316L) resist it, which is why they are chosen for welded work.
Austenitic stainless expands about 1.5 times as much as mild steel and conducts heat poorly, so it **distorts** more: clamp well and keep the heat input low.
Ferritic stainless suffers grain growth in the HAZ, which makes it less tough. Martensitic stainless cracks easily and needs preheat and heat treatment after welding.
Particles of carbon steel from grinding discs, wire brushes, tools, slings, racks or nearby grinding sparks stick to stainless and **rust on its surface**, leaving brown stains and starting pits.
Keep stainless on its own racks, with its own tools, iron-free discs and stainless wire brushes, and lift it with fabric slings or covered forks.
After welding, the heat tint is removed by pickling and passivating, or by mechanical cleaning, as the procedure says. Pickling chemicals are hazardous: follow their safety data sheet.
Light: about **one third** of the weight of steel for the same size. Not magnetic, and makes no sparks when cut.

Its **oxide film** melts at about 2000 °C, far hotter than the aluminium (about 660 °C), so it is removed with a stainless wire brush and solvent just before welding, and by the cleaning action of the AC TIG arc. Left on, it causes lack of fusion.
It conducts heat about **4 times** as well as steel, so it needs more heat input, or preheat on thick sections.
It expands about **twice** as much as steel, so it distorts more: clamp, tack and plan the welding sequence.
It does **not change colour** before it melts, so the welder watches the pool closely.
Hydrogen from damp, grease or dirty filler causes **porosity**: keep everything clean and dry.
It clogs abrasive discs and saw blades, so keep discs and blades for aluminium only.
**Heat-treatable** alloys (for example 6061 and 6063) and **work-hardened** alloys (for example 5083 marine plate) both lose some strength in the HAZ.

head: Metal
Made of
Properties
Uses
Joining
rows: Excellent conductor of heat and electricity; ductile; resists corrosion
Electrical work, water pipes, heat exchangers
Brazing and soldering; thick copper needs a lot of heat or preheat to weld
Brazing; when welded the zinc boils off as fume (metal fume fever)
Copper and tin (also aluminium bronze, phosphor bronze)

blocks.p: **Zinc** is used for galvanising and die castings; **lead** for flashings (it is poisonous); **nickel** in alloys and in electrodes for cast iron.

head: Kind
Behaviour
Examples
rows: Soften when heated and harden when cooled, again and again, so they can be **heat-welded** (hot-plate fusion for HDPE pipe, hot air for PVC)
Set hard for good when first cured; cannot be melted again or welded; char when heated
Two materials combined: fibres carry the load and a matrix binds them
GRP (glass fibres in resin), carbon fibre, reinforced concrete

blocks.note: Never cut or heat PVC with a torch, an arc or a hot abrasive disc: burning PVC gives off hydrogen chloride and other toxic fumes. Read the safety data sheet of any plastic or coated material before cutting or heating it.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Steel rusts when **oxygen and water** reach it. **Salt** (chlorides) speeds rusting up greatly, and so do high humidity and places where water and dirt lie, such as crevices and unsealed joints.

When **two different metals touch** and are both wet with an electrolyte, such as salty rain or sea spray, they act like a battery. The **less noble** metal (the anode) corrodes faster, and the **more noble** metal (the cathode) is protected.

head: Galvanic series in sea water (simplified)
Behaviour
rows: Corrode when joined to the metals below them
Stainless steel (with its oxide film), titanium

ul: The **further apart** two metals are in the series, the worse the corrosion.

**Area matters.** A small anode joined to a large cathode corrodes fastest: aluminium rivets in a large stainless panel waste away quickly, while stainless screws in a large aluminium sheet do much less harm (though they should still be insulated).

**Prevent it:** choose metals close together in the series, or the same metal for fasteners and parts; separate different metals with insulating washers, sleeves, gaskets or sealant; paint both metals, and if only one can be painted, paint the more noble one; design joints to drain; use zinc as a sacrificial coating or anode.

blocks.p: Stainless steel and aluminium depend on their oxide film. **Chlorides** from salt break the film at small points, making small, deep holes: **pitting**. In **crevices** (under washers, in gaps, in pockets where water and sand lie) oxygen cannot reach the surface to renew the film, so **crevice corrosion** starts there. Avoid crevices or seal them, design so water drains away, choose 316 or duplex near the sea, and wash coastal stainless regularly with fresh water.

head: Method
How it works
Points to know
rows: A barrier of primer, undercoat and topcoat
Surface preparation matters most: clean to bare metal, remove spatter, slag and flux
The finished item is dipped in molten zinc (about 450 °C), coating it inside and out
Zinc corrodes first and protects scratches (sacrificial protection). Hollow sections need **vent and drain holes**: trapped air or moisture can burst violently in the hot zinc bath
Repairs galvanising after welding or cutting
Clean the area to bright metal first
The longest life near the sea
Zinc or aluminium blocks fixed to hulls and tanks corrode instead of the steel
Replace them as they waste away
Drain holes, no water traps, joints sealed by continuous welds, no crevices

blocks.note: Salt-laden sea breeze reaches most of Jamaica's coastal towns, and many hotels, docks and homes stand right on the shore. For coastal steelwork, use galvanising plus paint (or 316 stainless), seal-weld joints so water cannot get in, and design so water drains away.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Heat treatment is heating and cooling steel in a controlled way to change its properties. The result depends on the **carbon content**, the **temperature reached** and, above all, the **rate of cooling**.

head: Treatment
How it is done
Result
Where you meet it
rows: Heat to the hardening range (red heat), hold, then cool **very slowly**, in the furnace or buried in dry sand or ash
As soft and ductile as possible; stresses removed
Softening tool steel so it can be filed or machined; before heavy forming
Heat to about the same temperature, then cool in **still air**
A finer, more even grain; a little stronger and harder than annealed
Heat medium or high carbon steel to its hardening temperature (often a bright cherry red, roughly 780–850 °C depending on the carbon), then **quench** in water, brine or oil
Reheat hardened steel to a lower temperature (about 200–350 °C for tools; higher for tougher parts), then cool
Some hardness and brittleness taken away; tougher
Heat a welded part to below the hardening range (for carbon steel often about 550–650 °C), hold, then cool slowly
Lowers the stresses locked in by welding: less distortion when machined, less risk of cracking
Thick welded frames, pressure parts, as the procedure says
Add carbon to the surface of low carbon steel at high temperature, then quench; or flame or induction harden the surface of medium carbon steel
A hard, wear-resisting surface on a tough core

blocks.p: **Mild steel** has too little carbon to form much martensite, so quenching it does not make it hard. To give it a hard surface, it is **case hardened**.

When hardened steel is polished and gently reheated, oxide colours appear on the bright surface in a fixed order as the temperature rises. Tempering stops when the right colour reaches the working edge.
Charts differ a little: follow the one your instructor uses. Judge colours in shade, not in bright sunlight.

ul: Hold the work in **tongs** and lower it in steadily, moving it about; stand to one side of the tank, away from steam and spatter.
Quench in oil only if the instructor allows it: hot oil can flash and catch fire. Keep a lid and an extinguisher at hand, and never pour water into hot oil.
Wear a face shield, heat-resistant gloves and a leather apron.
Hot steel looks exactly like cold steel once it stops glowing: mark it HOT and leave it to cool on the hearth.

head: Sample
File test
Bend test in the vice
rows: Bends well; a little stiffer than annealed
Snaps with little or no bend; fine grey fracture
Bends a little or springs back; much tougher than hardened

blocks.note: Wear safety glasses for bend tests: hardened samples can snap and fly. Keep every sample labelled so each result can be traced to its treatment.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Method
What it tells you
Limits
rows: Markings, stencils, labels and heat number
The grade, and the link to the certificate
Can wear off or be cut off
The grade, by the stockist's or Centre's own code
There is no single national code: check the chart
Carbon steel, cast iron, ferritic and martensitic stainless are magnetic; austenitic stainless, aluminium, copper and brass are not
Cannot tell carbon steel from ferritic stainless; cold-worked austenitic can be slightly magnetic
Copper red-brown, brass yellow, aluminium light silver-grey, galvanising spangled, mill scale blue-black
Coatings and dirt hide the metal
Aluminium is about a third of steel; copper and brass are heavier than steel

Mild steel: long straw-coloured streaks with few forks. Higher carbon: more, bushier, star-like bursts. Cast iron: short, dull red streaks. Stainless: shorter orange streaks with few bursts. Aluminium, copper, brass: no sparks
A guide only; compare with known samples
Hardness; cast iron chips crumble and its fracture is grey; steel chips curl
Portable alloy analyser or laboratory analysis
Costs money; used for important jobs

blocks.p: The steel maker issues a **mill test certificate** for each heat (cast) of steel. It gives the standard and grade, the **heat number**, the size, the chemical analysis (and often the CE), and the mechanical test results: yield strength, tensile strength, elongation and, where ordered, impact values. Check that the heat number on the steel matches the certificate, and that the results meet the specification.

flow: Check the delivery against the purchase order and delivery note: grade, size, quantity, condition
Check the certificates and match each heat number
Book the material into the register
Store it on marked racks, with stainless and aluminium apart from carbon steel
Quarantine unmarked or doubtful material until its grade is confirmed
Before cutting, transfer the grade and heat number to each part and to the offcut
Record the heat numbers on the cutting list or job card
File the certificates with the job records

blocks.p: If a fault is found later, these records show where the material came from, and which other parts were made from the same heat.

ul: Store steel off the ground, on racks, under cover and dry.
Secure long bars so they cannot roll or fall.
Keep stainless and aluminium on separate racks, protected with timber or plastic.
Keep plastics out of the sun, which weakens them.
Keep the safety data sheets for coated materials, paints and plastics.

blocks.note: Mass (kg) = volume (m³) × density (kg/m³). Change millimetres to metres first (divide by 1000).
blocks.label: Remember

head: Item
Working
Mass
rows: Steel round bar Ø30, 3 m long

blocks.p: Tables give the mass per metre of standard sections, allowing for their rounded corners. Masses are needed to plan lifts and choose slings, to order and price steel, and to plan transport.

head: Factor
Questions to ask
rows: What loads must it carry? What sizes will that need?
Indoors or out? Near the sea? Chemicals or water?
Can the shop weld and finish it well? How much will it distort?
Must it be light, or be carried by hand?
Material, fabrication, finish and maintenance over its whole life
Is it in stock locally? How long to get it?
Can the owner keep it painted, or wash it?
What finish does the client want?

blocks.p: **Section shape matters too.** A hollow section (RHS, SHS or CHS) resists bending and buckling much better than a solid bar of the same mass, because more of its metal is far from the centre. An I-beam is best for bending in one direction.

Example: a ramp handrail for a clinic in Mandeville, inland in cool, wet hills. Hot-dip galvanised and painted mild steel tube is strong, cheap, easy to weld and repair locally, and the galvanising deals with the damp. Stainless would cost far more for little gain so far from salt spray.
Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and work through it with your instructor.

ul: I can sort materials into ferrous, non-ferrous and non-metal groups, and carbon steels by their carbon content.
I can describe the kinds of cast iron and where each is used.
I can explain mechanical and physical properties in the right terms.
I can work out stress, strain, elongation, modulus and factor of safety.
I can describe a tensile test and explain yield strength, proof stress, UTS, necking and elongation.
I can compare the Brinell, Vickers and Rockwell hardness tests and the Charpy impact test.
I can explain what a bend test shows.
I can explain the HAZ, carbon equivalent and hydrogen cracking, and how preheat and low-hydrogen welding help.
I can describe how cast iron is welded.
I can compare austenitic, ferritic, martensitic and duplex stainless steels, and explain L grades and grade 316.
I can keep stainless steel free of carbon steel contamination.
I can explain how aluminium and copper alloys behave when cut and welded.
I can tell thermoplastics, thermosets and composites apart, and handle PVC safely.
I can explain rusting, galvanic, pitting and crevice corrosion, and how to prevent them.
I can explain annealing, normalising, hardening, tempering, stress relieving and case hardening, and test the results.

c1.title: Sorting an offcut rack in Black River
c1.text: Stacy-Ann is sorting unmarked offcuts at a training centre in Black River, St Elizabeth. Bar A is strongly attracted by a magnet and, touched on the bench grinder, gives bright, bushy sparks with many star-like bursts. Plate C is dull silver-grey, not magnetic, measures 300 × 200 × 10 mm and weighs about 1.6 kg. Piece E is magnetic, and when it is filed its chips crumble to grey powder. The rack also holds offcuts of PVC pipe.

c2.title: A mill certificate for a footbridge near Christiana
c2.text: Omari is checking the mill certificate for 12 mm plate delivered for a footbridge that the municipal corporation is building near Christiana, Manchester. It gives: yield strength 290 N/mm², tensile strength 445 N/mm², elongation 26%, carbon 0.16%, manganese 1.05%, carbon equivalent 0.36, and heat number 7A2214, which matches the number stencilled on the plates. The engineer's design keeps the working stress in the main plates to 120 N/mm².

c3.title: Balcony railings at a hotel in Runaway Bay
c3.text: A hotel in Runaway Bay, St Ann, is replacing balcony railings a few metres from the sea. The old 304 stainless rails are pitted, and their post bases sit in pockets where rainwater and sand collect. The new 316 rails were ground on site with discs that had been used on mild steel, and within weeks they show rust spots. The design includes aluminium glass channels and galvanised mild steel brackets, some made from closed hollow sections.

c4.title: Making cold chisels in Yallahs
c4.text: At a training centre in Yallahs, St Thomas, Renee's group is making cold chisels from tool-steel bar with about 0.8% carbon. They forge the point, soften the bar so it can be filed to shape, harden the tip and then temper it. One chisel was quenched and then used without tempering, and its edge shattered on the first blow. A trainee asks why they cannot make chisels the same way from mild steel bar.

c5.title: Two farm repairs near Frankfield
c5.text: A farmer near Frankfield, Clarendon, brings two jobs to the workshop: a grey cast-iron pump housing with a crack in one flange, and a 40 mm shaft of medium carbon steel (about 0.45% carbon) whose worn bearing seat must be built up with weld. On a trial build-up, made in a breeze with no preheat, a file skates over the metal next to the weld.

questions.q: What do bar A's sparks suggest, compared with mild steel?
o: It has less carbon than mild steel
It is a stainless steel
It has more carbon than mild steel
It is a cast iron
questions.why: Higher carbon steels give more, bushier, star-like bursts than mild steel, which gives long streaks with few forks. Cast iron gives short dull red streaks, and stainless gives shorter streaks with few bursts.

questions.q: Which metal is plate C most likely to be?
o: Brass
Aluminium
Copper
Mild steel
questions.why: Its volume is 0.3 × 0.2 × 0.01 = 0.0006 m³. In aluminium (2700 kg/m³) that weighs about 1.6 kg; in steel it would be about 4.7 kg, and brass or copper heavier still. It is also non-magnetic and silver-grey.

questions.q: What is piece E most likely to be?
o: Austenitic stainless
Medium carbon steel
Hard aluminium alloy
Grey cast iron
questions.why: Grey cast iron is magnetic, and its graphite flakes make filings crumble to a grey powder instead of curling like steel chips. Austenitic stainless and aluminium are not magnetic.

questions.q: A trainee wants to cut the PVC offcuts to size quickly with the oxy-fuel torch. Why must he not?
o: The PVC would melt the torch's nozzle
Burning PVC gives off toxic fumes
The flame would harden the PVC for good
PVC cannot be cut by any heat method
questions.why: Heated or burning PVC gives off hydrogen chloride and other toxic fumes. Cut plastics with saws or cutters made for them, and read the safety data sheet before heating any plastic.

questions.q: What is the factor of safety on yield in the main plates?
o: About 3.7
About 1.5
About 0.4
About 2.4
questions.why: Factor of safety on yield = yield strength ÷ working stress = 290 ÷ 120 ≈ 2.4. Dividing the tensile strength instead (445 ÷ 120) gives 3.7, which is the factor on tensile strength, not yield.

questions.q: What does the carbon equivalent of 0.36 suggest about welding this 12 mm plate?
o: It should weld well, usually with no preheat
It cannot be welded at all without full heat treatment
It must be preheated to red heat before every run
It will crack whatever electrodes or preheat are used
questions.why: A CE below about 0.40 means the steel does not harden strongly, so it usually welds without preheat at ordinary thicknesses. The WPS still sets the actual preheat and consumables.

questions.q: The plates will be cut into many smaller parts. How should traceability be kept?
o: Keep only the certificate, as all of the plate is one grade
Mark the heat number on each part and on the offcut
Write the heat number on the delivery note only
Mark the heat number only on the largest cut piece
questions.why: Transferring the heat number to every part and offcut before cutting keeps each piece linked to its certificate. If a fault is found later, every part from that heat can be found.

questions.q: In a test on this steel, a stress of 100 N/mm² gives a strain of 0.0005. What is its modulus of elasticity?
o: 20 000 N/mm²
50 000 N/mm²
questions.why: Modulus = stress ÷ strain = 100 ÷ 0.0005 = 200 000 N/mm² (200 GPa), the usual figure for steel. It measures stiffness, not strength.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the rust spots on the new 316 rails?
o: Grade 316 cannot stand up to any salt spray
The molybdenum in 316 rusts in sea air
Iron particles from the mild-steel discs
The rails were never welded right round
questions.why: Discs used on carbon steel leave iron particles on the stainless surface, and these rust in the salt air, staining it and starting pits. Stainless needs its own iron-free discs and tools.

questions.q: Which joint would corrode fastest in the sea air if left uninsulated?
o: Stainless screws holding a large aluminium sheet
Aluminium rivets holding a large stainless panel
Stainless screws holding a stainless rail
Aluminium rivets holding a large aluminium sheet
questions.why: In a galvanic couple the less noble metal corrodes, and a small anode joined to a large cathode corrodes fastest. Small aluminium rivets in a big stainless panel waste away quickly.

questions.q: Before the hollow-section brackets are hot-dip galvanised, what must the fabricator make sure of?
o: That closed sections have vent and drain holes
That every closed section is sealed fully airtight
That every bracket is painted with primer first
That the welds are ground flush on every bracket
questions.why: Air or moisture trapped in a closed section expands violently in the hot zinc bath and can burst the section. Vent and drain holes also let zinc coat the inside and drain out.

questions.q: What is the best way to stop the new posts corroding at their bases like the old ones?
o: Paint over the bases each year with fresh paint
Fill the pockets with sand to keep water out
Change the posts to 304 so they rust more slowly
Design the bases so water drains away
questions.why: Water and sand trapped in pockets starve the surface of oxygen and hold salt against it, causing crevice and pitting corrosion. Designing out the crevice works better than any coating.

questions.q: Why did the untempered chisel's edge shatter?
o: It had been annealed and was too soft
Its carbon was burnt out in the forge
It was left fully hard and brittle
It was quenched in water, not oil
questions.why: Quenching leaves tool steel at its hardest and most brittle. Tempering takes away some hardness and makes it tough enough to take blows.

questions.q: How should the group soften the forged bar so it can be filed to shape?
o: Heat it to red and quench it in water
Heat it gently until it shows a purple colour
Heat it to red and cool it very slowly in ash
Heat it to red and cool it in moving air
questions.why: Annealing (heating to red heat and cooling very slowly, buried in dry ash or sand) makes steel as soft as possible. Cooling in air is normalising, and quenching hardens it.

questions.q: Why can a chisel not be made the same way from mild steel bar?
o: Mild steel melts at a much lower heat
It has too little carbon to harden much
Mild steel cracks as soon as it is forged
It can only be hardened by quenching in oil
questions.why: With only about 0.1–0.25% carbon, mild steel forms little martensite when quenched, so it stays fairly soft. Its surface can be hardened only by case hardening.

questions.q: As the polished tip is gently reheated for tempering, which colour appears first?
o: Deep purple
Dark blue
Light brown
Pale straw
questions.why: As the temperature rises the colours appear in order: pale straw, dark straw, brown, purple, then blue. Tempering stops when the colour the chart gives reaches the cutting edge.

questions.q: Which approach is usual for welding the crack in the cast-iron housing?
o: Mild steel electrodes in long, fast, hot runs
Short nickel-electrode runs, each peened
Quench each weld run in water so it toughens
Weld it cold in one long run, with no cleaning
questions.why: Cast iron is brittle and cracks under welding stress. Nickel-based electrodes give soft weld metal, and short runs, peening and slow cooling keep the stresses low; preheating the whole casting is the other method.

questions.q: Why does the file skate over the metal next to the trial weld on the shaft?
o: Weld spatter has coated the surface
The heat drew carbon out of the shaft
The HAZ hardened as it cooled quickly
The file is too blunt for any steel
questions.why: A medium carbon steel cooled fast from welding heat forms hard martensite in the HAZ, and the breeze and lack of preheat speeded the cooling. Preheat and low-hydrogen welding are needed to stop it cracking.

questions.q: Junior must lift a 2 m piece of Ø40 round bar onto the saw. Roughly how heavy is it? (Take steel as 7850 kg/m³.)
o: About 19.7 kg
About 9.9 kg
About 78.9 kg
About 25.1 kg
questions.why: Area = 3.142 × 20² = 1257 mm² = 0.001257 m²; volume = 0.001257 × 2 = 0.002514 m³; mass = 0.002514 × 7850 ≈ 19.7 kg. Using the diameter instead of the radius gives four times too much.

questions.q: Why are aluminium and stainless steel usually given a 0.2% proof stress instead of a yield point?
o: They have no clear yield point
They break before they stretch at all
Their yield point is above their UTS
Proof stress is only used for cast metals
questions.why: Unlike mild steel, these metals pass from elastic to plastic stretching gradually, with no clear yield point. The proof stress is the stress that leaves a set permanent stretch, often 0.2%.
